title: Misfit Ventures aims to tap into charitable giving with new donor-advised fund
html:
Misfit Ventures is launching its own donor-advised fund (DAF) with the help of fellow Vancouver organization Charitable Impact Foundation as it looks to convince more high-net-worth individuals to put their capital behind LGBTQ+ technology entrepreneurs.

The venture capital (VC) firm revealed Misfits Foundation on stage last Thursday during QueerTech’s latest annual conference. The two-day event, the largest in Canada for members of the LGBTQ+ community working in tech, brought over 700 people to Toronto’s Evergreen Brick Works to discuss inclusive AI and other topics from a variety of perspectives.

“I’m willing to be that guinea pig of trying something new to try and get more capital into the ecosystem.”

Misfit, which is currently raising its inaugural fund, claims to be Canada’s first and North America’s largest VC firm focused on LGBTQ+ founders building in tech, while Charitable Impact is a registered charity and public foundation that offers an online platform for individuals, families, and organizations to manage their charitable giving from a single account.

“There [are] a lot of [HNW] individuals that we’ve approached … or we’ve been introduced to, for potential investment, [who] really just don’t understand the [VC] world, so they want to stay away from it,” Misfit co-founder and managing partner Mandy Potter told BetaKit in an interview. “But what they do understand is donating.”

That realization was a driving factor behind Misfit’s decision to launch the Misfits Foundation DAF under Charitable Impact. Another was the state of the VC fundraising market, which has been particularly challenging for emerging managers and impact funds like Misfit, which has set out to finance LGBTQ+ and other historically underrepresented entrepreneurs at the earliest stages.

Potter described trying to raise a first fund in this environment as “fucking impossible” during her remarks on stage. “It’s the hardest thing I’ve ever done,” she added.

While Misfit’s new DAF was built “in a selfish way in the sense that we needed to find different avenues for capital,” Potter said her intentions are pure. “I want to see more impact funds and new fund managers be successful, so I’m willing to be that guinea pig of trying something new to try and get more capital into the ecosystem.”

RELATED: “A perfect storm”: 2025 was the worst year for Canadian VC fundraising since 2016

In Canada, a DAF is a fund established by a charity to which others donate and help guide. This structure permits donors to collectively give to multiple causes from the same account. Potter and fellow Misfit co-founder and managing partner Douglas Lui are leading the initiative.

Dollars donated to Misfit’s DAF will be held by Charitable Impact, while the fund’s strategy and giving will be guided by Potter. Those donations will be invested into Misfit’s core fund and deployed into startups with LGBTQ+ leadership. Potter said the firm’s DAF has already secured commitments, but declined to share how much exactly to date.

Unlike limited partners (LPs) investing in Misfit’s fund, individuals who donate to this DAF will receive an immediate charitable tax receipt from Charitable Impact. Any returns generated on the capital that Misfit invests from this DAF will remain committed to charity and be redistributed to other causes at the discretion of Misfit’s leadership team.

QueerTech board chair Bradley Breton, who previously served as chief of staff at Toronto FinTech firm Zafin, is a Misfit LP. For donors, he said this DAF offers a means for folks interested in maximizing their impact on LGBTQ+ communities while also reaping the associated tax benefits, whereas becoming a Misfit LP provides a pathway that balances that impact with financial returns.

RELATED: Queer tech founders explore move to Canada as US abandons DEI

Breton is also one of the champions of another DAF focused on LGBTQ+ communities through Charitable Impact called Q Impact. Launched by Breton, founding donor Barry Inouye, a former leader at Amazon and Coca-Cola, and Trevor Loke, a community ambassador at Charitable Impact.

Q Impact is a cause fund, a structure that Kirsten Hurlbut, account manager at Charitable Impact, said allows people “to come together and support the cause instead of the organization.”

“The goal is to create a sustainable cause fund that can support the queer community across different policy issues, both nationally and internationally,” Breton told BetaKit in an interview.

Dollars donated to Q Impact are held by Charitable Impact. According to Q Impact’s website, the cause fund has secured more than $1.3 million to date.

Charitable Impact also helps power another such fund dedicated to promoting therapies for those living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.

Potter is hoping that Misfit’s DAF can serve as a model for other emerging managers and impact funds. Breton said QueerTech is also exploring how to use DAF-based giving to support some of its own programming.

Feature image courtesy QueerTech. Photo by Naomi Silver-Vézina.
summary: Amid a tough fundraising market, the LGBTQ+ VC firm is trialling a new way of bringing individuals into the fold. The post Misfit Ventures aims to tap into charitable giving with new donor-advised fund first appeared on BetaKit .
